content:
A common challenge runs like this. Moses parted the sea and Jesus raised the dead, but the Quran itself admits that Muhammad (peace be upon him) brought no miracles. When his opponents asked for a sign, the critic says, he answered that he was "only a warner." A prophet without signs, the argument goes, has no credentials.

The challenge rests on real verses, and it deserves a careful answer. The six answers below set out what the Quran says about signs, what it presents as the Prophet's sign, what the hadith report, and what a miracle can and cannot prove. Each objection is stated at full strength first.

The critics quote the Quran accurately. "Those who disbelieve say: Why is a sign not sent down to him from his Lord? You are only a warner, and every people has a guide" (13:7). "They say: Why are signs not sent down to him from his Lord? Say: The signs are with God alone, and I am only a clear warner" (29:50).

In 17:90-93 the Quraysh list what they want to see: a spring gushing from the ground, a garden of palms and vines, the sky falling on them in pieces, God and the angels brought before them, a house of gold, a ladder into the sky with a book they could read. The answer given is: "Glory be to my Lord. Am I anything but a human being, a messenger?"[1]

So it is true that the Quran records demands for signs that were refused. A Muslim reader gains nothing by pretending otherwise. The question is what those refusals mean, and the Quran explains them itself.

The fullest explanation is in 17:59: "Nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them. We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign, and they wronged her. We send the signs only as a warning." In the Quran's account, a people who demanded a sign, received it and then rejected it were destroyed, as Thamud were after they killed the camel. On this account, refusing the demanded signs was a mercy to Mecca, which was spared the fate of Thamud.[2]

A second reason is given in 6:109. The opponents swore that they would believe if a sign came. The reply: "Signs are with God. And how do you know that if it came, they would not believe?" A third runs through the whole book: no messenger brings a sign at his own command.

"It was not for any messenger to bring a sign except by God's permission" (40:78). Even the miracles of Jesus, which the Quran affirms in detail, are done "by God's permission" (3:49).[2]

The Gospels report the same pattern. When the Pharisees asked Jesus for a sign from heaven, Mark says that "he sighed deeply in his spirit and said, 'Why does this generation seek a sign? Truly, I say to you, no sign will be given to this generation'" (Mark 8:12). Matthew gives the saying as "An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah" (Matthew 12:39).

A refusal to perform on demand does not show that Jesus worked no miracles. It does not show it of Muhammad either.[3]

The same passage that says "I am only a clear warner" goes on: "Is it not enough for them that We have sent down to you the Book, which is recited to them?" (29:51). The Quran offers itself as the sign, and it puts the claim in a form that can be tested: "If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to Our servant, then bring a chapter like it, and call your witnesses besides God, if you are truthful" (2:23).[4]

The Prophet described his mission in the same terms. In a report in Sahih al-Bukhari he said: "Every prophet was given signs because of which people believed, but what I have been given is the revelation which God has revealed to me. So I hope that my followers will outnumber the followers of the other prophets on the Day of Resurrection."[5]

The difference matters. A sign such as the parting of the sea convinced those who saw it, and every later generation has to take it on report.

A book that claims to be its own evidence can be read, recited and tested by anyone in any century. The site's article on the claim of grammatical errors in the Quran takes up one of the ways critics have tried to meet the challenge.

It is not quite true that the Quran claims no physical sign. Surah 54 opens: "The Hour has drawn near and the moon was split. And if they see a sign, they turn away and say: Passing magic" (54:1-2). The second verse treats the first as something the Meccans saw and dismissed.[6]

The hadith collections report the event from several companions. In Bukhari, Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud says: "During the lifetime of the Prophet the moon was split into two parts, and on that the Prophet said: Bear witness." Anas ibn Malik relates that the people of Mecca asked the Prophet to show them a sign, and he showed them the splitting of the moon.[7]

Two concessions belong here. No record outside the Muslim sources describes the event, and a few later commentators read 54:1 as a sign still to come at the end of time. The majority of the commentators, who had the reports of Ibn Mas'ud and Anas before them, read it as past.

The absence of an outside record is less telling than it sounds: a sight in the night sky over Arabia had no reason to enter the chronicles of distant peoples. The site's article on the claim that Muhammad was a false prophet sets out the grading of these reports and the early reading that took the verse as a sign of the Last Hour.

The moon is not the only event the Quran itself describes. Of the battle of Badr, where a small Muslim force met a far larger army, it says: "You did not kill them, but God killed them; and you did not throw when you threw, but God threw" (8:17).

The commentators connect the verse with the handful of dust the Prophet threw toward the enemy at the start of the battle. The Quran ascribes the outcome to God, as it ascribes every sign, and it presents Badr as a sign to those who saw it: "There was a sign for you in the two forces that met" (3:13).[6]

Beyond the moon, the collections preserve reports of other signs, told by different companions about different occasions. Jabir ibn Abd Allah relates that at Hudaybiyya the people had no water except a small vessel, and that the Prophet put his hand in it and water flowed between his fingers until some fifteen hundred people had drunk and washed.

Anas relates that a small quantity of barley bread, sent by Umm Sulaym, fed a large gathering. Jabir relates that during the digging of the trench at Medina a small meal fed the whole company of workers.[8]

The best known of these is the palm trunk. Ibn Umar relates that the Prophet used to give his sermons standing beside the trunk of a date palm.

When a pulpit was made and he moved to it, the trunk cried, and the Prophet went to it and passed his hand over it. Jabir adds that it "cried like a child" until he embraced it.[9]

Later scholars gathered these reports into whole books. Al-Bayhaqi, in the eleventh century, compiled his Dala'il al-Nubuwwa, "The Proofs of Prophethood," in several volumes, with the chain of narrators for each report, so that a reader could weigh them one by one. The collection is a sign of how the tradition treated these reports: as evidence to be examined, with sound and weak reports kept apart.[10]

Each of these reports, taken alone, is the report of one or a few narrators, and a critic can question any one of them. The scholars who collected them made a different point.

Qadi Iyad, in his work on the qualities of the Prophet, argued that the signs come through so many companions, on so many occasions, that their general meaning is established even where a single report might be doubted. The careful position is between the two: the Quran does not rest the Prophet's claim on these reports, and Muslims do not need to defend every one of them to hold that the Prophet was given signs.[10]

The challenge assumes that signs are the test of a prophet. The Bible does not agree. Deuteronomy warns that a prophet may give "a sign or a wonder, and the sign or wonder that he tells you comes to pass," and still be false if he says "Let us go after other gods" (Deuteronomy 13:1-3).

Jesus warns that "false christs and false prophets will arise and perform great signs and wonders, so as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect" (Matthew 24:24). John's Gospel says of John the Baptist, whom Jesus called more than a prophet: "John did no sign, but everything that John said about this man was true" (John 10:41).[11]

The Quran applies the same test. What it asks of a messenger is a message consistent with what earlier prophets brought: the oneness of God, His justice and the coming judgement. Al-Faruqi describes faith in Islam as conviction reached through evidence, open to counterevidence, and the Quran's challenge in 2:23 is the kind of evidence that remains open to examination.[12]

The bottom line

The Quran does record demands for signs that were refused, and the critics quote those verses correctly. It also explains the refusals: a sign demanded and then rejected brings destruction, and no messenger works signs at his own command.

The Gospels record Jesus refusing signs on the same terms. The Quran offers itself as the Prophet's sign, reports the splitting of the moon, and the companions report further signs that the scholars collected with care.

None of this makes a miracle the final test. Moses, Jesus and Muhammad all taught that wonders can mislead and that the message is what must be weighed.

The Quran puts its message forward and invites the reader to test it. God knows best.

Notes

  1. Quran 13:7; 29:50; 17:90–93.
  2. Quran 17:59; 6:109; 40:78; 3:49. On Thamud and the she-camel, compare 7:73–79 and 91:11–15.
  3. Mark 8:11–12; Matthew 12:38–39 and 16:1–4. Bible quotations follow the English Standard Version.
  4. Quran 29:51; 2:23–24; compare 10:38, 11:13 and 17:88.
  5. Sahih al-Bukhari 4981, Book of the Virtues of the Quran, report of Abu Hurayra.
  6. Quran 54:1–2; 8:17; 3:13
  7. Sahih al-Bukhari 3636 (Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud) and 3637 (Anas ibn Malik), Book of the Virtues and Merits of the Prophet.
  8. Sahih al-Bukhari 3576 (Jabir, the water at Hudaybiyya), 3578 (Anas, the bread of Umm Sulaym) and 4101 (Jabir, the meal at the trench).
  9. Sahih al-Bukhari 3583 (Ibn Umar) and 3584 (Jabir), on the crying palm trunk.
  10. Qadi Iyad ibn Musa al-Yahsubi, al-Shifa bi-Ta'rif Huquq al-Mustafa, part one, the chapter on the miracles of the Prophet; al-Bayhaqi, Dala'il al-Nubuwwa.
  11. Deuteronomy 13:1–3; Matthew 24:24; John 10:41; compare Matthew 11:9–11.
  12. Ismail Raji al-Faruqi, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life, 2nd edition (Herndon: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 1992), chapter 4, section III.
